Time in practice Select One 1 ≤5 years O [CONTINUE] 2 6-10 years O [CONTINUE] 3 11-20 years O [CONTINUE] 4 >20 years O [CONTINUE] QUALIFICATION: Qualified Congratulations – you have qualified for this study! Non-Qualified Thank you for your willingness to participate. Due to the specific guidelines for this study, we are unable to include you. We look forward to your involvement in future research studies. MAIN SURVEY: Show each domain topic on separate screen; Show below question text on all main survey screens. Freeze header at top of grid. Provide open text box [‘Please explain your answer’] for each statement, if respondent selects ‘Tend to disagree’, ‘Disagree’ or ‘Strongly Disagree’.Please review each statement and indicate your level of agreement with it (only one tick box per statement). If you disagree with a statement, please explain your answer. Please only complete this survey once. Completion should take no longer than ~15 minutes and all responses received are anonymous. Topic No. Statement Level of Agreement Strongly Agree Agree Tend to Agree Tend to Disagree Disagree Strongly Disagree Burden and impact of head and neck involvement in moderate-severe AD Psychological burden and impact on quality of life Moderate-severe atopic dermatitis with head and neck involvement is associated with a disproportionate patient burden, particularly due to the visibility of the disease and its psychological impact ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement can have a significant impact on patient quality of life (QoL) ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ The psychological and quality-of-life burden of AD with head and neck involvement is frequently under-recognised in clinical practice, leading to underestimation of disease severity and undertreatment ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement can have a significant impact on patient confidence and social engagement due to the visibility of the condition, impacting relationships and intimacy ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Patients with moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement often require significant time off work and disruption to education due to the physical and mental burden of the condition ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Patients with moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement experience disruption to sleep and daily activities due to the physical and mental burden of the condition. ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Head and neck involvement should be actively assessed at the first specialist consultation in patients with atopic dermatitis, including both clinical severity and psychological impact ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Assessing patient burden in clinical practice Clinicians often have limited time to properly assess the burden of moderate-severe AD on the patient ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Clinicians do not always have the required education or tools to properly assess the burden of moderate-severe AD on the patient ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ The psychological burden and QoL impacts of AD with head and neck involvement should be assessed using validated scoring systems such as DLQI or HADS ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Clinical challenges in managing head and neck AD Key features, symptoms or patient history for clinical suspicion of AD with head and neck involvement A history of patient or familial atopy or eczema (including childhood eczema) combined with symptoms of facial itch, burning, stinging, or scaling should prompt clinical suspicion of AD with head and neck involvement ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Moderate-severe AD with head and neck may flare upon infection ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Moderate-severe AD with head and neck may flare upon use of cosmetics ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Moderate-severe AD with head and neck may flare upon exposure to airborne allergens ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Moderate-severe AD with head and neck may flare upon exposure to UV light ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Moderate-severe AD with head and neck may flare upon either the application or the withdrawal of topical steroids ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Core clinical parameters to identify moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement Clinicians should use scoring systems that have specific criteria for the face and neck region, such as EASI, in addition to more global and holistic scores like HADS, PPNRS, DLQI etc, when evaluating patients with AD with head and neck involvement ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Head and neck involvement may be exacerbated by environmental, topical, or treatment-related factors, which should be considered during assessment ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Patch testing for airborne allergens such as house dust mites, pollens and pet dander should be performed when there is clinical suspicion of moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Common overlapping conditions and forming a diagnosis Seborrheic dermatitis and seborrheic psoriasis should be ruled out by examination of distribution (i.e. in seborrheic zones), scalp scale, and nature of inflammation (itching, lichenification, excoriation) ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Allergic contact dermatitis should be ruled out with patch testing, IgE blood testing or a skin prick test if clinically indicated ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Concomitant irritant contact dermatitis should be pragmatically managed by irritant avoidance and general skin care in patients with AD with head and neck involvement ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Potential for and consequences of late discussion and diagnosis AD with head and neck involvement can be overlooked throughout the treatment pathway due to a perceived lack of severity ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ AD with head and neck involvement in patients with skin of colour is commonly underrecognised, as erythema and inflammation can be less visible ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ There is more likely to be problematic lichenification and post inflammatory hyperpigmentation for patients who have deeper skin tones with AD with head and neck involvement due to late diagnosis and under treatment ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Delayed diagnosis or suboptimal management of moderate-severe head and neck AD can result in prolonged disease activity, increased psychological burden, and poorer long-term outcomes. ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Identification and management of head and neck AD in adults and adolescents Treatment of adolescents should be similar to that of adults, but should consider different triggers or stressors, such as hormonal changes and increased physical activity ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Adult-onset head and neck AD requires more in-depth investigations for potential alternative or co-existing diagnoses ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Head and neck involvement should be considered early in the treatment pathway and may justify more proactive or escalated treatment strategies at first consultation. ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Current treatment pathways for head and neck AD and their limitations Current treatments for moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement The use of dupilumab can be associated with worsened disease on the face and neck region ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ The prolonged use of high-potency topical corticosteroids on the face can lead to adverse events and should be used cautiously ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Main challenges and pitfalls with current treatment options in H&N AD While topical corticosteroids are offered as a first-line treatment for AD with head and neck involvement in-line with current guidance, earlier optimisation of systemic or targeted therapies may be appropriate in selected patients with significant head and neck involvement ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Arbitrary local EASI cut-offs and regional variations in commissioning criteria fail to account for the disproportionate impact of head and neck AD, leading to systemic undertreatment of patients who otherwise meet national systemic therapy guidelines ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Current guidelines lack specific recommendations for the long-term management of moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Despite available treatments, patients with head and neck atopic dermatitis may continue to represent an area of unmet need in clinical practice ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Follow-up of patients with moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement Head and neck involvement might be one factor to prompt a more timely initial follow up appointment ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Initial follow-up appointments should be every 6-12 weeks depending on the severity of the condition ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ After treatment initiation, follow-up appointments can be extended to every 3 months to assess treatment efficacy and disease progression ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Follow-up pathways for moderate-severe head and neck AD should be dynamic and tailored to control of the disease; well-controlled patients can transition to extended or annual reviews, supported by a Patient-Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) mechanism to allow rapid access during flares ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Management of new symptoms or “flare-ups” that arise from treatments for existing AD Patch testing and review of the original diagnosis should be considered when new head and neck symptoms arise from treatments used for existing AD ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Oral antifungal therapy should be employed for head and neck AD flares when clinical signs and symptoms, such as refractory facial erythema, scaling, and severe itching suggest secondary yeast involvement or a Malassezia driving phenotype ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Topical treatments should be utilised to manage head and neck flares that present as paradoxical redness or residual disease despite successful systemic therapy ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ A switch to an alternative biologic or a JAK inhibitor may be considered when head and neck flares present as paradoxical redness or residual disease that fails to respond to topical interventions during existing systemic therapy ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Managing patients through flare-ups between treatments or when beginning a new treatment (“bridging” therapy) When initiating a new treatment or switching between treatments, intensive topical treatments are needed to manage flare-ups while medication is continued ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Managing flare-ups between treatments or when beginning a new treatment requires careful, patient-specific consideration, including disease severity, to plan effective bridging strategies and prevent the worsening of flare-ups ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Defining priorities to address unmet needs in head and neck AD Guidance for AD with head and neck involvement Improved guidance for the identification of AD with head and neck involvement should include more specific screening and evaluation tools for use across different skin tones ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Improved guidance for the management of AD with head and neck involvement should include practical management advice, such as which tests to perform and when and general skin care advice ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Improved guidance for the management of moderate-severe AD with head and neck involvement should include first-line recommendations for targeted treatments of the head and neck region, based on patient groups, contraindications, and severity of the disease ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ AD with head and neck involvement represents a clinically meaningful presentation with specific challenges characterised by increased disease burden, treatment resistance, and the need for tailored management approaches ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ AD with head and neck involvement should be defined using the Hannifin and Rajka criteria (with patients having >3 major and/or minor symptoms, including itch, erythema, scaling oedema, lichenification or photosensitivity), with the disease affecting the eyelids, cheeks, scalp, or neck ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Management of AD with head and neck involvement should include consideration of psychological comorbidities and appropriate support or referral where needed ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Primary and secondary care education Primary and secondary care education should improve awareness of various clinical presentations (i.e. across different skin tones), psychological comorbidities, and identification of differential diagnoses ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ Primary and secondary care education for AD with head and neck involvement should improve awareness of treatments available and when best to employ different treatment options (i.e. topical treatments, biologics or JAK inhibitors) ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ ¢ CLOSING NOTE TO PROVIDE THE RESPONDENT Thank you for taking the time to complete this survey. Your insight will be invaluable to this Delphi project. This research has been commissioned by LEO Pharma.

A UK Delphi Consensus on Atopic Dermatitis with Head and Neck InvolvementFIRST SCREEN:
IntroductionFollowing a Delphi consensus, the aim of this project is to build consensus to improve the clinical management of atopic dermatitis (AD) with head and neck (H&N) involvement.
To help us achieve this, we are inviting you to review the first round of consensus statements that were developed by a panel of experts forming a steering committee (hereafter referred to as the expert committee) of healthcare professionals, based on an initial evidence review.
This double blinded project has been initiated and funded by a pharmaceutical company and is being managed and delivered by Triducive Partners Ltd (an independent specialist healthcare consultancy). We are required by the General Data Protection Regulation to reveal the name of the sponsoring company, and do not intend that this should influence you in any way. We will share this information at the end of the survey.
This is a closed question survey, and the purpose is to measure level of agreement with the consensus statements.
Consent for participation will be implied by completion of the survey. The information provided by the participants will be used for the stated specified purposes only. An individual's responses will not be used in any way that would allow their identification. All completed questionnaires will be collected by M3 Global, a market research organisation, and analysed by Triducive. Anonymous responses will be provided in an aggregated form to the expert panel and sponsoring company.
For further information about how Triducive protects your personal information and how you may exercise your data protection rights, you can contact Triducive at info@triducive.com or visit https://triducive.com/privacy-policy/.
